title: Applying Core Pricing Methods in Practice
description: Practice identifying and applying cost-plus, value-based, and competitive pricing strategies in realistic business scenarios.

interactions.prompt: A bakery's cupcakes cost $1.50 to make. They price at $3.75. A competitor sells similar cupcakes at $3.00. What pricing signal matters most here?

options.text: They're using value-based pricing tied to brand perception
They're using cost-plus pricing with a 150% markup
They're underpricing relative to competitor benchmarks
They're pricing above competitors, risking lost volume

interactions.prompt: When a SaaS company prices its product based on how much time and money it saves customers, it is using ____ pricing.

options.text: Cost-plus
Competitive
Value-based
Penetration

interactions.prompt: You're launching a new coffee brand. Starbucks charges $5 for a latte, local shops charge $3.50. Your costs are $1.20. Do you price at $3.25 or $4.50?

options.text: $3.25 — undercut competitors to build volume quickly
$4.50 — position between premium and local for credibility
$3.25 — match local shops and compete on convenience
$4.50 — higher price signals quality to justify the brand

interactions.prompt: Slack's free tier has 10K message history. When surveyed, 68% of teams say they'd pay to avoid losing messages. Only 22% cite advanced features as their reason to upgrade. What's the key pricing insight?

options.text: Slack should lower its price to convert more free users
Pain of data loss drives willingness to pay, not features
Slack should add more features to justify premium pricing
Most users will never convert so free tier should shrink

chartData.title: Primary Reasons Teams Upgrade from Free Tier

interactions.prompt: A startup selling project management software needs to set its initial price. Rank these steps from first to last in a sound pricing process.

options.text: Calculate your unit costs and desired margin
Research competitor pricing and positioning
Survey target customers on willingness to pay
Set and test your final price in the market

interactions.prompt: Your B2B analytics tool costs $8/user to deliver. Enterprise clients say it saves them $200/user/month in analyst time. You currently charge $25/user. A competitor just launched at $20/user. What do you do?

options.text: Drop to $19/user to undercut the new competitor
Stay at $25 — your value delivered far exceeds the price
Raise to $50 — capture more of the $200 value created
Match at $20 and add a premium tier at $40

interactions.prompt: A luxury skincare brand is evaluating pricing factors. Rank these from most to least important for their pricing decision.

options.text: Raw material and production costs
Perceived brand prestige and exclusivity
Price sensitivity of target affluent customers
Competitor pricing at drugstore brands

interactions.prompt: A sudden tariff doubles your raw material costs overnight. Your $50 product now costs $35 to make instead of $18. Your competitor hasn't raised prices yet. What's your best move?

options.text: Immediately raise to $67 to preserve your original margin
Hold price, absorb the hit, and wait for competitors to move
Raise modestly to $60, communicate the tariff transparently
Cut features to reduce costs back to $18 per unit

interactions.priorContext: You previously set your price at $50 using cost-plus with a healthy margin on $18 costs. Now a tariff has nearly doubled your costs to $35, compressing your margin to just $15 while competitors haven't adjusted yet.
